title: A US-China-Russia Summit: What’s at Stake?
content:
Vladimir Putin’s proposal for a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Donald J. Trump on the margins of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit is alarming on two counts.

At first blush, it raises the specter of a new Yalta, and it threatens talks on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine without Ukraine and its European allies at the table.

Yet that may not prove the greatest consequence — such a meeting would most likely prove inconsequential, because a deal along those lines would almost certainly run counter to Xi’s and Trump’s more immediate interests (including their desire not to fixate on Ukraine or be upstaged by Putin).

Where it could prove consequential is in how the world interprets it.
snippet: Vladimir Putin’s proposal for a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Donald J. Trump on the margins of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit is alarming on two counts.
creator: Kinsey Burr

title: Rebuilding Ukraine: A Testing Ground for Western Innovation?
content:
Missiles rain down over Ukraine’s cities. Drones devastate the expanding battlefield. Although reconstruction may seem far off, the West needs to prepare for gigantic infrastructure projects, estimated to cost at least $590 billion over a decade. And that’s without counting additional devastation.

It will be a giant challenge for a labor-starved, financially strapped, war-torn country. But Ukraine’s needs could become a giant opportunity — provided that the country leverages artificial intelligence, robots, and drones.

The obstacles start with personnel. After widespread emigration and war deaths, Ukraine has only about half of the skilled construction workers it needs for reconstruction, a shortfall of up to 800,000 workers. Russia is deliberately destroying Ukraine’s production capacity: recent strikes shut down the country’s two largest steel mills, causing steel production to fall by more than half.

title: EU Tech Rules Pit Privacy Against Competition
content:
After running two half marathons, I decided to get serious and buy a sports watch. As an iPhone owner, I wanted to know if a watch from another manufacturer would work well with my phone. 

That simple question exposes a crucial tension in European tech policy. On the one hand, Europeans pride themselves on producing the world’s most powerful digital privacy rules, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). On the other hand, they pride themselves on producing the world’s most powerful rules around sharing data. The Digital Markets Act (DMA) requires Apple and other “gatekeepers” to open their devices to competing products in the name of consumer choice and market competitiveness.  

But there’s a giant problem: the two sets of rules often fight with each other.

title: Serbia’s New Government Needs New Security Services
content:
Now that Aleksandar Vučić’s government is gone, evicted by joyous voters, EU leaders will be wondering how to approach Serbia’s new administration.

What can the West offer? There will no doubt be many answers, but the best is to encourage root-and-branch reform of the country’s over-mighty and outdated security system.

The election victory changes the government and provides a strong political mandate, but it will not automatically affect the agencies at the heart of government. The state remains the same until the people, rules and assumptions in the intelligence services and the army change. That is why the first serious test of the new government will be the security sector, and not the distribution of ministries.
snippet: Now that Aleksandar Vučić’s government is gone, evicted by joyous voters, EU leaders will be wondering how to approach Serbia’s new administration.
creator: Kinsey Burr

title: Exiled Russian Musicians Fill Arenas to Inspire the Lost Generation
content:
Hundreds of thousands of Russians have left their homeland since 2022, and among them are artists who publicly condemn the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Despite being labeled foreign agents and prohibited from re-entering Russia, they keep playing shows in Asia, Europe, and North America.

As anti-war Russians in exile search for new cultural identities beyond Putin’s regime, the concerts serve as rallying points for their country’s lost generation.

Yelizaveta Gyrdymova, known by her stage name Monetochka, is at the forefront of Russian artists speaking out against the war. Banned from returning to Moscow, Monetochka continues touring abroad , where her performances attract thousands of diaspora Russians.

In her recent releases, such as “Это было в России” (It was In Russia), she evokes strong feelings of nostalgia in her audience by recalling fond everyday memories from the country she loves but is no longer allowed to call home.

title: Serbia’s New Government Has a Mountain to Climb
content:
There is something in the air in Central Europe, and it smells like change. After the landslide victory of Hungary’s Péter Magyar in April, the Student List ousted Serbia’s long-time strongman Aleksandar Vučić with a convincing electoral win on October 25.

Even so, it will prove difficult to relaunch the country’s democratization process and navigate international waters after 12 years of illiberal, Kremlin-friendly Vučić rule.

As with Viktor Orbán in Hungary, there had been much discussion of a Belarus-style theft of the result using the security forces to beat down the winners. As with Orbán, this did not happen. Instead, at around 9:30 p.m. on election night, Vučić took the stage and conceded defeat. He had lost by 53% to 39%, and his opponents had secured a working parliamentary majority from the highest turnout for 34 years.

Across Serbia, the initial shock was followed by wild celebrations that continued late into the night, and the capital city of Belgrade suddenly became a scene of public joy not seen since the ousting of the president and war criminal Slobodan Milošević in 2000, after he attempted to steal an election.

title: Russia’s Drone Incursions Multiply in Moldova
content:
Russian drones have crossed into Moldovan airspace more frequently in 2026 than at any time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago.

Chișinău International Airport has been forced to suspend operations for spells to protect civilian aviation, and Moldovan authorities have admitted that, while they can detect the drones, they lack the capacity to intercept them.

A French radar system bought with public money, and another with European Union assistance, sound the alarm, but Moldova does not have the resources for military jets or other systems to shoot them down.

Neighboring Romania has F-16 fighters, but Moldova cannot benefit from their support because its neutrality blocks such military cooperation.

The Air Operation Service of the national army reported at least 81 cases of Russian drone incursions in the past four years. The frequency of such incidents grew gradually from a few cases in 2022 to more than 40 so far this year. Six missiles have also been detected.

The majority were believed to be heading for targets in Ukraine and deviated into Moldovan airspace.
snippet: Russian drones have crossed into Moldovan airspace more frequently in 2026 than at any time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago.
creator: Kinsey Burr

title: Russia’s Ministry of Control
content:
These have been good years for Putin’s security overlords. The war against Ukraine has licensed growing domestic repression and paranoia, and that has empowered the secret police in ways that were hard to imagine even a decade ago.

This spring, rumors began to circulate that the FSB’s gaze had now fixed on the Ministry of Digital Development and that some of its responsibilities could be transferred. This came amid reports that the FSB’s Second Service, responsible for repressing political dissent, was taking related steps to establish control over the internet industry.

In seeming confirmation of these reports, key figures in Russia’s cybersecurity industry, including Natalya Kaspersky, a prominent IT entrepreneur and former wife of the cybersecurity entrepreneur Eugene Kaspersky, discovered that the Second Service had compiled reports on them. This week, Russian news agencies reported that the ministry would soon get a new deputy head: a serving FSB officer.

title: Action Needed to Get Ukraine’s Grain to the World
content:
Russian attacks on seaports and commercial vessels in the Odesa region and the Danube Delta have critically reduced Ukraine’s grain corridor after three years of successful operation.

The 2026 harvest needs to be sold and, while Ukraine and its partners have developed alternative routes, none come close to the volumes or costs of sea transportation.

Agricultural produce accounts for 60% of Ukraine’s exports, and 90% are usually carried by sea, underlining the importance of the corridor to the country’s beleaguered economy.

While Russia increases its attacks, it is important to focus not only on resolving the current situation, but also on a strategic plan to reorient Ukraine’s industry and economy to a different model. Without change, depleted grain exports will trigger an even larger chain of economic and food crises next year.

As of October, Ukrainian granaries were almost full, and there was a critical shortage of free capacity for late crops.

The issue of storage can be temporarily resolved with the help of alternative solutions, such as polymer grain sleeves, but such temporary workarounds do not address the risks if space cannot be freed up.

title: Nostalgic Nightmares in Romania
content:
When I visited Romania as a young journalist during the winter of 1986, the capital Bucharest’s streets were dark. The stores were empty. The little available food was inedible. After it snowed, the country’s communist dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu banned cars and buses, leaving sad, fur-capped Romanians to fill the streets, sullenly walking to work. On my second visit in early 1989, the Securitate secret police arrested and expelled me for attempting to interview a dissident.

This summer, I returned to celebrate a good friend’s 40th birthday. My multilingual friend and his wife had worked with cutting-edge tech companies. At his birthday party, the crowd of multilingual young professionals, often educated abroad, resembled a gathering of upwardly mobile people in Paris, London, or any other Western capital. As we enjoyed fine food and wine, I marveled at how they enjoyed the same opportunities as my own privileged children.
